exam: What clinical features distinguish IPF from chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis? — Look for exposure history, BAL lymphocytosis, and HRCT distribution (upper‑mid vs basal).

A 58‑year‑old miner presents with progressive dyspnoea, basal crackles, and HRCT showing honey‑comb. What is your next step? — Confirm UIP pattern, exclude secondary causes, and start antifibrotic therapy.
How does the GAP score influence prognosis and management? — Higher GAP stage predicts mortality; guides timing of transplant referral and intensity of follow‑up.
Why is nintedanib preferred over pirfenidone in a patient with liver cirrhosis? — Both are antifibrotic, but pirfenidone is hepatotoxic; nintedanib has less hepatic metabolism.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate hospital admission? — Acute exacerbation with rapid dyspnoea, new ground‑glass opacities, and hypoxia.
Explain why a normal chest X‑ray does not rule out early IPF. — Early interstitial changes are subtle; HRCT is required for detection.
In a resource‑limited setting without HRCT, how would you approach suspected IPF? — Use clinical picture, chest X‑ray, PFTs, exclude infections, and consider empirical antifibrotic referral.
What are contraindications to lung transplantation in IPF? — Active infection, uncontrolled malignancy, severe comorbidities, or poor adherence.
ai.title: Interstitial Pulmonary Fibrosis
related: Acute Exacerbation of Interstitial Lung Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Chronic, progressive scarring of the lung interstitium leads to restrictive physiology and impaired gas exchange. Diagnosis relies on clinical context, imaging and exclusion of other causes. Management focuses on removing triggers, slowing progression and supportive care.

b: HRCT showing usual interstitial pneumonia pattern (basal, subpleural reticulation, honey‑comb, traction bronchiectasis)
Exclusion of known causes (occupational, drug, connective tissue disease, infection)
Multidisciplinary discussion (clinician, radiologist, pathologist) required
sections.p: Idiopathic interstitial pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a specific form of chronic, progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia of unknown cause, limited to the lungs.

b: Stage I: GAP score 0–3, FVC ≥ 75 % predicted, DLCO ≥ 55 % predicted
Stage II: GAP score 4–5, FVC 50–74 %, DLCO 36–54 %
Stage III: GAP score ≥6, FVC < 50 % or DLCO < 35 %
sections.p: Severity is graded by physiologic and radiologic indices; the GAP model (Gender‑Age‑Physiology) predicts mortality.

b: Asbestos exposure (occupational, e.g., brake‑liner workers)
Silica dust (mining, sandblasting)
Chronic infections: untreated pulmonary TB, HIV‑related opportunistic pneumonias
Drug‑induced: amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, anti‑TNF agents
Connective‑tissue disease: systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis
sections.p: When a cause is identified, the disease is termed secondary interstitial lung disease; in low‑resource settings, common triggers must be considered first.

b: Progressive exertional dyspnoea over months
Non‑productive cough
Fine inspiratory crackles (Velcro‑like) at lung bases
Digital clubbing in ~30 % of cases
sections.p: Patients develop insidious dyspnoea and dry cough; early disease may be silent.

t.b: What pattern of lung involvement is present? – Typical UIP pattern confirms diagnosis; absence suggests alternative ILD.

t.a: Pulmonary function tests (spirometry, lung volumes, DLCO)
t.b: What is the severity of restriction and gas‑exchange impairment? – Reduced FVC and DLCO indicate disease stage.
Is there an underlying connective‑tissue disease? – Positive auto‑antibodies shift diagnosis to secondary ILD.
Is infection or alveolar haemorrhage present? – Lymphocytosis suggests hypersensitivity pneumonitis; neutrophilia may indicate infection.
If unavailable, rely on multidisciplinary consensus and treat as probable IPF.

b: Acute exacerbation (rapid worsening, new ground‑glass opacities, high mortality)
Pulmonary hypertension leading to right‑heart failure
Cor pulmonale
Superimposed infection (pneumonia, TB re‑activation)
Respiratory failure requiring supplemental O₂ or ventilation
sections.p: Complications can be rapidly fatal and require urgent attention.

b: Eliminate exposure (asbestos, silica, offending drugs)
Antifibrotics: nintedanib or pirfenidone – slow FVC decline; avoid if severe liver disease or pregnancy
Vaccinations: influenza, pneumococcal, COVID‑19
Supplemental O₂ to maintain SpO₂ ≥ 90 % at rest and during activity
Pulmonary rehabilitation to improve exercise tolerance
Consider lung transplantation in eligible patients
sections.p: Therapy combines removal of triggers, antifibrotic drugs, and supportive measures.

b: Clinic review every 3–6 months with PFTs and symptom assessment
Repeat HRCT only if clinical change suggests acute exacerbation
Educate on smoking cessation, avoidance of dust, and early infection reporting
Screen for pulmonary hypertension if dyspnoea out of proportion to PFT decline
sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression and complications early.

b: Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis – often has exposure history, BAL lymphocytosis
Sarcoidosis – nodular infiltrates, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, non‑caseating granulomas
Non‑specific interstitial pneumonia – ground‑glass predominance, better response to steroids
Post‑TB fibrosis – history of treated TB, localized scarring rather than diffuse UIP
sections.p: Several interstitial and obstructive diseases mimic IPF clinically and radiologically.

b: Normal chest X‑ray early in disease – HRCT required for detection
Mildly reduced DLCO may be attributed to anemia; correct for haemoglobin
Positive ANA in isolation does not prove connective‑tissue disease; correlate clinically
sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls are common in low‑resource settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness or new chest pain (possible acute exacerbation)
Rapid drop in oxygen saturation below 85 % despite supplemental O₂
Signs of right‑heart failure (edema, jugular venous distension) developing quickly
